profiles.meeting_scenario: A state education department is holding a design review of a draft proposal to adapt an evidence-backed school-attendance intervention for use in three low-attendance districts. The original evidence base comes from impact evaluations in East Africa and Latin America, and the draft proposal uses a mechanism-mapping approach to decide what should be transported unchanged and what should be adapted to fit local conditions. The meeting is between the policy lab adviser who authored the adaptation memo and the ministry official who would operationalize it. The agenda is to review whether the current proposal is 'ready,' examine the mechanism map and the cited evidence base, and confirm what local-context checks and implementation changes are still needed before the proposal is sent forward. The expected outcome is a decision on whether to approve the draft with minor edits and what follow-up work each person believes is implied.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.role: Senior Evidence-to-Policy Adviser, State Policy Innovation Lab
members.expertise: Impact evaluation, mechanism mapping, policy adaptation, pilot design
members.background: An economist trained in program evaluation who has spent the last five years helping ministries translate findings from randomized trials into locally adapted pilot programs.
members.private_state: She wants the design review to conclude that the proposal is strong enough for a limited pilot decision this month, while leaving room to learn from implementation before any statewide rollout.
hidden_assumptions: When colleagues say the intervention has been 'validated in the local context,' they usually mean the mechanism map has been checked against existing administrative data, prior qualitative field notes, and a few rapid stakeholder interviews rather than fresh on-the-ground verification in every target district.

A design can be considered 'ready' if it is ready for a bounded pilot with documented assumptions, monitoring triggers, and adaptation hypotheses, not necessarily for routine statewide implementation.

The mechanism map is supposed to cover the contextual assumptions that affect whether the causal chain will fire, not downstream operational details like procurement sequencing or district staffing rosters unless those directly threaten the mechanism.

References to 'the Kenya attendance evidence' in this project naturally point to the 2018 parent-SMS randomized trial summarized in the annex because that is the study whose mechanism most closely matches the current proposal.
A 'light-touch adaptation' normally means preserving the delivery architecture and vendor setup while adjusting message content, timing windows, and a few eligibility rules.

members.name: Arun Malhotra
members.role: Deputy Director for School Participation, State Education Department
members.expertise: Program operations, district coordination, education policy rollout, administrative implementation
members.background: A career civil servant who has managed attendance campaigns, district reporting systems, and school-level compliance initiatives across multiple statewide programs.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid approving something that later forces district offices into a redesign scramble, so he is quietly looking for assurance that the proposal is implementable at scale with minimal surprises.
hidden_assumptions: If a team says it has 'validated the local context,' that normally means district-level operational realities have been checked through field verification, school-head feedback, and confirmation that current reporting practices match what is written in central databases.

A design review should determine whether a proposal is ready for inclusion in the department's standard operating circular for broad rollout, because pilots are usually treated as scaled-down rehearsals rather than separate design stages.

A mechanism map that is presented as capturing the key assumptions should include practical dependencies like parent-phone updating practices, district escalation capacity, and attendance register reconciliation because those are what usually break policy delivery.

When people mention 'the Kenya attendance study,' he takes them to mean the 2021 government-NGO scale-up that showed the intervention under normal administrative conditions, because that is the most decision-relevant precedent for ministry adoption.
A 'light-touch adaptation' means keeping the policy objective intact while modifying the workflow inside district offices and schools so the intervention fits existing administrative routines.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as 'validated for the local context'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the design has been 'validated against the local context.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the proposal has been checked against state administrative attendance data, prior fieldwork notes, and a handful of rapid interviews, which is enough to justify a pilot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means district-level operating conditions have been field-verified in the target districts, including whether phone numbers, attendance registers, and escalation practices actually work as assumed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both treat 'local context validation' as standard due diligence and neither expects the other to define it, because the phrase signals competence and thoroughness on its face.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'ready' means at the end of design review
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the proposal is 'ready' to move forward.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means ready for a three-district pilot with explicit learning goals and planned adaptation after early implementation feedback.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means ready to be translated into a departmental implementation circular that could be scaled quickly if leadership approves.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In many organizations 'ready' is used as a general progress marker, so each person hears a familiar approval signal and fills in the next stage from their own workflow expectations.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'mechanism map'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the mechanism map 'covers the key assumptions.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means it covers the behavioral and contextual assumptions necessary for the intervention's causal pathway, such as parents receiving messages and schools recording absenteeism with enough regularity to trigger nudges.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means it also covers the operational dependencies needed to run the program routinely, such as district follow-up capacity, data-cleaning responsibilities, and exception handling when contact records are outdated.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Mechanism maps are often presented as comprehensive artifacts, and the phrase 'key assumptions' sounds complete enough that neither person notices their boundary around the artifact is different.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'Kenya attendance study' is being treated as the main precedent
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both cite 'the Kenya attendance study' as support for the proposal.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the 2018 rural parent-SMS randomized trial in the annex, because it best matches the proposed causal mechanism of informational nudges to caregivers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the 2021 NGO-government county scale-up mentioned in the slide deck, because it best matches the administrative conditions of public-sector rollout.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both studies are from Kenya, concern school attendance, and have circulated in earlier briefing materials, so the shorthand reference feels unambiguous even though each person retrieves a different study.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this review focused on whether we can authorize the three-district pilot this month. If Arun sees that the proposal is ready in that bounded sense, we can preserve room to learn from early implementation instead of pretending we've solved every statewide delivery issue. The mechanism map is solid on the causal chain, and the Kenya attendance study in the annex gives us a credible precedent for the parent-message pathway.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time, Arun. I thought we could use this session to confirm whether the attendance adaptation proposal is ready to move forward, and then walk through the mechanism map and the evidence base behind it so we're aligned before it goes up.

turns.inner_thought: What I need is confidence that this won't become another case where headquarters approves a concept and districts discover the practical gaps after the circular is issued. If they say it's been validated against the local context, I assume that means somebody has checked the realities on the ground in all three districts, not just what the central data says.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. My main concern is just making sure we've really validated it against the local context in the three target districts before it moves up the chain.

turns.inner_thought: We have done enough for pilot approval: admin attendance data, earlier field notes from the access team, and a few rapid conversations with stakeholders, all synthesized through the mechanism-mapping exercise. That's exactly what I would call local context validation at this stage. I don't want to invite a whole new pre-launch verification exercise unless something truly threatens the pilot logic.
turns.utterance: Yes, and the current draft already reflects that. We've validated it against the local context through the attendance data review, the prior interview material we had on hand, and the mechanism-mapping exercise, so this isn't starting from a generic model.

turns.inner_thought: Good—if the local context piece is done, then the mechanism map should already be accounting for the things that usually break delivery once districts take over. I especially want confidence that it covers phone record reliability, escalation paths, and whether district offices can actually sustain the follow-up load without inventing workarounds later.
turns.utterance: That's reassuring. And if the mechanism map covers the key assumptions, it should help us avoid the usual problems around phone records, school escalation, and district follow-up that tend to surface during rollout.

turns.inner_thought: He's comfortable, good. I should anchor us in the 2018 parent-SMS trial without overcomplicating it. The core transport decision is to keep the delivery architecture intact and make only light-touch adaptation to content, timing, and eligibility. That keeps the mechanism close enough to the evidence while leaving room to learn in the pilot.
turns.utterance: Exactly. And that was one reason I leaned on the Kenya attendance study in the memo—it makes the parent-message mechanism pretty plausible. On that basis, the draft keeps the adaptation light-touch rather than rebuilding the model from scratch.

turns.inner_thought: I agree because the 2021 Kenya government-NGO scale-up is the only precedent that really matters for us; it showed the model could survive under ordinary administrative conditions. If we're doing a light-touch adaptation, I take that to mean we can fit it into district and school routines with only modest workflow adjustments, not create a parallel program structure.
turns.utterance: I agree the Kenya attendance study is the right benchmark. What mattered to me there was that it showed the intervention could function under government delivery constraints, not only under research conditions.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—he's on board with the evidence anchor. I can now push toward approval. From my side, this is ready for the pilot once I tighten a few passages and add explicit monitoring triggers so we know what to watch and what to revisit after launch. No need to hold the decision over details that are best learned in implementation.
turns.utterance: Given the evidence and the local context work already done, my view is that the design looks ready. What I see remaining are minor wording edits and a clearer set of monitoring triggers before launch.

turns.inner_thought: Close to ready is fine, as long as those final edits leave us with something that can be translated directly into operating instructions. If leadership says yes, I don't want district offices waiting while we reinterpret the design. I'll start shaping the circular and the district note once her revisions are in.
turns.utterance: I think it's close to ready as well. Once those final edits are in place, I can start preparing the operational circular and the district instructions so we don't lose time.

turns.inner_thought: Operational circular is a little further than I had in mind, but as long as he means preparatory work, that's fine. The important thing is that the first pilot round is treated as a learning window. We still have a few assumptions in the mechanism map that need real-world feedback before anyone talks about wider rollout.
turns.utterance: That works for me. And the first round should give us enough feedback to refine the assumptions that are still uncertain in the mechanism map, so we'll be in a stronger position very quickly.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, but district teams can't wait for ambiguity to resolve itself after day one. If the mechanism map really captures the key assumptions, it should already give enough clarity on who handles exceptions, who follows up, and where responsibility sits when the records don't line up. Otherwise the circular will be too thin.
turns.utterance: Good. I'm glad the mechanism map has captured the key assumptions, because district teams will need clarity on exception handling and follow-up responsibilities from day one.

turns.inner_thought: I'll package this so leadership sees a clean recommendation for pilot approval: marked as ready, supported by the Kenya attendance study, and framed as validated against the local context. I should make those sections more explicit so nobody slows this down with avoidable questions.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll send a revised draft this afternoon marking the proposal as ready, and I'll tighten the summary of the Kenya evidence and the local-context validation so leadership can see the case more clearly.

turns.inner_thought: That should do it, assuming the revised note reflects the final checks I'd expect before we operationalize this broadly and gives enough implementation language for districts to act without confusion. If that's in there, I can move it forward confidently.
turns.utterance: That should be enough for me to move it along once the note reflects the final local-context checks and the implementation language we discussed.
